canonical_statement: The study aimed to characterize UFH dosing and safety across differing severities of cirrhosis during treatment of VTE and to assess whether cirrhosis severity is associated with different UFH dose requirements to achieve therapeutic anti-Xa levels.
This was a single-center retrospective observational study at the University of Michigan Medical Center covering October 1, 2014 through December 31, 2017.

Eligible patients were adults with imaging- or biopsy-confirmed cirrhosis and proven or suspected VTE who received a UFH infusion for at least 48 hours and had anti-Xa levels documented after each dose change and at least daily.

population.label: Adults with cirrhosis treated with UFH for proven or suspected VTE
inclusion_criteria: Cirrhosis confirmed by MRI, ultrasound, CT, or biopsy
UFH infusion for at least 48 hours
Anti-Xa levels after each dose change and at least once daily

canonical_statement: Patients were excluded if they were younger than 18 years, pregnant, or had a coagulopathy known to alter anti-Xa monitoring, such as inborn factor X deficiency.

population.label: Study exclusion criteria
exclusion_criteria: Coagulopathy known to alter anti-Xa monitoring

canonical_statement: VTE was confirmed by Doppler venous ultrasound, chest CT, or physician documentation of high clinical suspicion when confirmatory studies were absent; cirrhosis was confirmed by imaging or biopsy.
UFH dosing was managed by pharmacists and/or nurses using an institution-specific anti-Xa-based heparin nomogram with a therapeutic anti-Xa target of 0.3-0.7 IU/mL.

exposures.details: Institution-specific anti-Xa-based nomogram; anti-Xa target 0.3-0.7 IU/mL

canonical_statement: Initial and subtherapeutic UFH boluses were administered according to the nomogram only when approved by the ordering physician.
Therapeutic UFH dosing was considered achieved after a second consecutive anti-Xa level within target, with the two levels drawn 6 hours apart.

outcome.definition: Two consecutive anti-Xa levels within the therapeutic range, drawn 6 hours apart

canonical_statement: The prespecified primary efficacy outcome was the mean UFH infusion rate in U/kg/h that resulted in two consecutive therapeutic anti-Xa levels.

concept.text: UFH infusion rate producing two consecutive therapeutic anti-Xa levels

canonical_statement: Secondary efficacy outcomes were the initial anti-Xa level after protocol-based UFH initiation, time to therapeutic anti-Xa, and the number of dose increases with or without bolus before therapeutic anti-Xa was reached.

outcome.definition: Initial anti-Xa, time to therapeutic anti-Xa, and dose increases/boluses before therapeutic anti-Xa

canonical_statement: Safety outcomes within 30 days of UFH initiation included newly identified thromboembolism, bleeding of any severity, death, and a composite endpoint containing all three.

outcome.definition: New thrombosis, any bleed including oozing/minor/major/life-threatening bleeding, death, and composite of these outcomes

canonical_statement: Decompensated cirrhosis was defined by physician documentation plus evidence including a history of ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, or esophageal varices.

Comparisons were performed by compensation status and by CTP class using parametric or nonparametric tests as appropriate; time-to-therapeutic anti-Xa was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier methods with 168 hours assigned as the surrogate endpoint for patients who never achieved consecutive therapeutic levels.
Of 74 screened patients, 51 were included; 23 were classified as compensated and 28 as decompensated cirrhosis.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that decompensated or CTP class C cirrhosis may be associated with a lower likelihood of reaching therapeutic anti-Xa levels than less severe cirrhosis.
The authors concluded that patients with more severe cirrhosis may require higher UFH doses to reach target anti-Xa levels, potentially increasing bleeding risk.
The authors suggested that general-population UFH nomograms and anti-Xa targets may be suboptimal for patients with decompensated cirrhosis and require further study.

The authors stated a preference for anti-Xa rather than aPTT monitoring of UFH in cirrhosis because aPTT can be discordantly elevated in this population, while acknowledging that anti-Xa may also be imperfect.
The authors recommended patient-specific multidisciplinary discussion of short- and long-term anticoagulation plans for cirrhotic patients with acute thrombosis.
The study was limited by its single-center retrospective design, small sample size, institution-specific UFH nomogram, and difficulties inherent in electronic medical-record interpretation.
The authors considered the study likely underpowered for most outcomes because of the small sample size.
Attribution of adverse events specifically to the UFH infusion could not be determined reliably from the retrospective record review.
Because the cohort included only patients with a prior diagnosis of cirrhosis, the study could not directly compare UFH response with patients having normal liver function.
The bleeding outcome included minor events such as oozing or epistaxis, and the analysis did not clearly separate all bleeding from major bleeding.
CTP and MELD scores could not be calculated for all patients because prior-to-admission warfarin affected INR; those patients were excluded from the corresponding score analyses.
The study reported no financial support for the research, authorship, or publication.
The authors reported no potential conflicts of interest related to the research, authorship, or publication.
